newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin says Chechen ties meet international norms.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin says Chechen ties meet international norms.

text.p: Russia, in a concession to Chechnya, has agreed to base its relations with the breakaway region on the norms of international law, according to a Kremlin statement issued on Monday after the signature of a peace accord.

"The two sides...agreed...to construct their relations in accordance with generally recognised principles and norms of international law," the statement released by the presidential press office said.
The Kremlin was quick to insist, however, that the use of the phrase "international law" did not mean Moscow was recognising Chechen independence from Russia.

President Boris Yeltsin and secessionist Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov signed the accord on Monday, pledging to end four centuries of conflict that culminated in a 21-month war that ended with a ceasefire last August.

The "Treaty on Peace and on Principles of Relations between the Russian Federation and the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria", the full text of which was not published, also committed both sides to abstaining from force or threats to resolve disputes.

The phrase "international law" appeared to be a concession by the Kremlin to the Chechen leadership, which has insisted on full independence from Russia by being recognised as a sovereign state under international law.

However, Yeltsin has made clear there will be no question of separating Chechnya from Russia. Disagreement over the final status of Chechnya threatened to bog down the peace process but the two sides agreed last August to leave it undefined for five years.
The phrasing of Monday's deal was apparently acceptable to Maskhadov while the Kremlin was able to insist it did not amount to a recognition of Chechnya's de facto autonomy.
Yeltsin's chief spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying the norms of international law were already incorporated in the Russian constitution.

Yastrzhembsky said that a key principle of international law was that the right of peoples to self-determination "should not conflict with the principle of territorial integrity of a state". As a result of this, he said, Monday's treaty did not deal with the issue of Chechnya's status.

"For the president of Russia, the question of the integrity of Russia has never been in doubt and will never be," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax, adding that Yeltsin had found an "appropriate non-classic solution" to a "non-classic situation".
